documents.title: Honor Code (includes Generative AI rule)
documents.stance_why: The Academic Resolutions say generative AI tools "should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work" unless an instructor "specifically and explicitly" authorizes it. That is ban-unless-permitted, so restrict, not delegates, because the default is set by the Code itself and instructors only grant exceptions.
documents.summary: The undergraduate Honor Code is a long student-governance document covering the Honor Board, hearing procedures, appeals and academic and social resolutions. A single paragraph in the academic resolutions sets the AI rule: no generative AI on coursework unless an instructor explicitly authorizes it, and undisclosed, unattributed or exam use is an Honor Code violation. The rest of the document supplies the general integrity and enforcement process that applies to such violations.

units.why: The sentence says generative AI tools "should not be used" for any assignments, exams or written work, so the default for all coursework is a ban. I chose P01 (default prohibition) over P06 because it does not address a silent syllabus; the permission mechanism is coded separately as P04.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools should not be used in the completion of any course assignments
units.policy: Generative AI tools should not be used in the completion of any course assignments, exams, or written work, including laboratory work, unless an instructor has specifically and explicitly authorized their use.

units.why: The exception "unless an instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized their use for the assignment in question" makes permission an instructor, per-assignment decision. This is P04 (who decides), not P06, since it names the decision-maker rather than the silent-syllabus fallback.
units.anchor: unless an instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized their use
units.policy: Generative AI use is allowed only where the instructor for a given course has specifically and explicitly authorized it for the assignment in question.

units.why: "Presenting AI-generated content as original student work" is named as a violation, which bars having AI produce what a student submits as their own. P19 fits better than P36 because the unit is the content of the prohibited act; the classification as a violation is coded separately.
units.anchor: Presenting AI-generated content as original student work

units.why: "submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools" makes uncited AI content a violation, so students must cite or disclose the AI source. P24 (disclose with each submission) fits; P28 would only fit if the passage discussed penalty effects of disclosure, and the violation label is coded in a separate unit.
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated content without citing its source
units.policy: Submitting AI-generated content without citing its source in artificial intelligence tools is a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: "relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams" is called a violation, so AI is barred in closed-book assessments. P22 is the exact type for no AI on exams and quizzes.
units.anchor: relying on generative AI tools for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams

units.why: The three listed acts "all constitute violations of the Honor Code", classifying improper AI use as an integrity breach handled by the Honor Board. P36 is right; concrete penalties are a separate type (P37) and are not given in this sentence.
units.anchor: all constitute violations of the Honor Code
units.policy: Presenting AI-generated content as original student work, submitting it without citing its source, and relying on generative AI for closed-book quizzes, tests, and exams all constitute violations of the Honor Code.

units.why: "Each student is responsible for the integrity of their own academic work" is a general ownership rule that the AI paragraph sits under, so it applies to AI-assisted work as well. P29 (students own what they submit) fits; it is not AI-specific, which I note here.
units.anchor: Each student is responsible for the integrity of their own academic work.

units.why: The Board "has the authority to justify any sanction up to failure of an examination or paper, failure of a course ... or expulsion", which are the penalties available for any Honor Code violation including AI misuse. P37 fits as stated penalty range, though it is not specific to AI.
units.anchor: authority to justify any sanction up to failure of an examination or paper
units.policy: The Honor Board has the authority to impose any sanction up to failure of an examination or paper, failure of a course, exclusion from a residence hall, exclusion from campus housing or expulsion from the College.

units.why: A person who suspects a violation "should talk in person with the student who committed the alleged violation" before any escalation, which is the talk-first step. P57 fits, and applies to AI cases as academic cases generally.
units.anchor: they should talk in person with the student who committed the alleged violation

units.why: Both parties "must write separate statements explaining the circumstances as they perceive them", giving the accused student a voice in the process. P64 (students may respond to allegations) fits, although it governs academic cases generally.
units.anchor: must write separate statements explaining the circumstances as they perceive them
units.policy: Both the confronting and confronted parties must write separate statements explaining the circumstances as they perceive them.

units.why: The Honor Board is responsible for "the periodic review of the Honor Code itself", which is a review cycle for the policy that contains the AI rule. P54 (revisit regularly) fits.
units.anchor: the periodic review of the Honor Code itself
units.frag_end: review of the Honor Code itself.

documents.title: Generative AI: Privacy and security guidelines (Ask Athena)
documents.stance_why: The page tells users to "Use College-provided AI tools" and to be careful with other tools, but sets no ban on AI and no per-course rule. It treats AI use as allowed with data, privacy and critical-evaluation conditions, so permit rather than delegates, and it defers academic limits to the Honor Code.
documents.summary: An IT help article on responsible use of generative AI with college data and systems. It points users to four college-provided tools, explains privacy and terms-of-service concerns, and warns about hallucination, bias, copyright, environmental cost and industry-sponsored claims. It tells students to follow the Honor Code and says nothing about course-level AI rules.

units.why: The page says the guidelines "support the responsible and ethical use of AI technology, while managing risk", stating the purpose of the framework. P56 (institution-level preamble) fits.
units.anchor: support the responsible and ethical use of AI technology

units.why: "Use College-provided AI tools (Firefly, BoodleBox, Microsoft Copilot, Zoom AI Companion)" directs users to vetted tools. I chose P50 (prefer vetted tools) over P17 because the point is the privacy reason for preferring them, not providing a course tool.
units.anchor: Use College-provided AI tools (Firefly, BoodleBox, Microsoft Copilot, Zoom AI Companion)

units.why: The note says provider terms ensure inputs and outputs "will not be used to train AI models or answer AI queries made by others", the factual basis for preferring the college tools. P50 covers protecting data and vetted tools.
units.anchor: will not be used to train AI models or answer AI queries made by others

units.why: "Other tools -- especially free ones -- may lack these protections" warns that non-college tools give weaker data protection; this is a privacy fact, so P50.
units.anchor: Other tools -- especially free ones -- may lack these protections

units.why: "Always review a tool's terms of service and privacy policies carefully" tells users to check terms before use, a data-protection step. P50 fits better than P52, which is about ownership and copyright of outputs.
units.anchor: Always review a tool's terms of service and privacy policies carefully

units.why: "if you must use free tools, avoid uploading private or sensitive information" limits what may be entered into non-vetted tools. P50 (protect personal data) is the match.
units.anchor: if you must use free tools, avoid uploading private or sensitive information

units.why: "Follow all relevant College policies: Acceptable Use Policy, Data Handling Policy" binds AI use to existing institution-wide policies. P56 (institution-wide framework) fits as it sets scope rather than a specific rule.
units.anchor: Follow all relevant College policies:
units.policy: Follow all relevant College policies, including the Acceptable Use Policy and the Data Handling Policy.

units.why: "Students must also adhere to their Honor Code" ties student AI use to the Honor Code and its academic limits. P56 fits as a scope statement; the AI rule itself lives in the Honor Code document.
units.anchor: Students must also adhere to their
units.policy: Students must also adhere to their Honor Code.

units.why: "Always critically evaluate any generative AI output." tells users to check AI output, which is the verify-output type. P31.
units.anchor: Always critically evaluate any generative AI output.

units.why: The tools are "vulnerable to biases in their training data" and "can predict things that are statistically plausible but inaccurate", including nonexistent citations. This explains why output must be verified, so P31; the bias mention is part of the same warning.
units.anchor: can predict things that are statistically plausible
units.frag_end: books and authors that do not exist!

units.why: "Look for settings that can help you critically evaluate a bot's output" suggests using tool modes that support checking, a way to act on the verification duty. P31 fits.
units.anchor: Look for settings that can help you critically evaluate a bot's output

units.why: "The applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to these tools is still under discussion" is a statement about legal uncertainty over AI inputs and outputs. P52 covers copyright and licensing.
units.anchor: applicability of copyright law,
units.policy: The applicability of copyright law, moral rights, and fair use to generative AI tools is still under discussion.

units.why: "Some generative AI products, such as Adobe Firefly, prohibit users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission" is a copyright and terms-of-use fact about uploading protected works. P52 over P49 because the rule belongs to the tool's terms, not a college ban.
units.anchor: prohibit users from uploading copyrighted materials without permission of the copyright holder

units.why: "AI processing is energy-intensive" with concern that AI growth will offset efficiency gains names an environmental cost. P53.
units.anchor: AI processing is energy-intensive

units.why: Readers are told to "think critically about who authored and published this information and what they stand to gain" regarding claims about AI impact. No type covers critical reading of industry-sponsored AI claims, so UNCOVERED; P31 is about verifying AI output, not AI-impact stories.
units.anchor: be sure to think critically about who authored and published this information
units.uncovered_note: Advice to read claims about AI's promises and perils critically, since sources may be sponsored by AI vendors (information literacy about AI discourse).

units.why: "The College reserves the right to disconnect or disable, without warning or prior notice, any computer, account, or service that poses a security or performance threat" is an enforcement power of IT, not about academic AI misuse. No type fits, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: reserves the right to disconnect or disable, without warning or prior notice
units.uncovered_note: IT security enforcement: the college may disable any computer, account or service that threatens resources or violates policy, without notice.

units.why: The list of college-provided tools describes BoodleBox as "a collaborative AI workspace with access to many LLM models and privacy and teaching features", naming sanctioned licensed tools. P17 fits as a provided tool.
units.anchor: A collaborative AI workspace with access to many LLM models
units.policy: The College provides BoodleBox AI, a collaborative AI workspace with access to many LLM models and privacy and teaching features, along with Adobe Firefly, Microsoft Copilot and Zoom AI Companion.

notes: Bryn Mawr has no computing or school AI policy found; the third collected document (LITS AI page) was screened out and not coded. The Honor Code AI paragraph is the only academic AI rule; the Honor Code's general procedures are coded only where they plainly apply to AI-related violations (P29, P37, P54, P57, P64 are not AI-specific). Topic codes come from tools/AGENT_BRIEF.md starter list.
